outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Case Setting, Technology, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the radio-frequency interference technology underlying the dispute, identifies the patents and accused functionality, and situates the appeal procedurally. It explains what passive intermodulation products are, why they matter in wireless systems, and how the case arrived at the Federal Circuit after a jury verdict and post-trial motions.
subtopics: The parties: Finesse Wireless as patent owner; AT&T and Nokia as accused infringers/appellants
The asserted patents: U.S. Patent Nos. 7,346,134 and 9,548,775
Basic technical background: intermodulation products (IMPs) and passive intermodulation (PIM)
Internal PIM versus external PIM and why that distinction matters to the accused radios
The accused feature: Nokia radios’ PIM cancellation (PIM-C) functionality used by AT&T
Trial outcome: jury findings of validity and infringement and the lump-sum damages award
Post-verdict motions: JMOL of noninfringement, JMOL on damages, and motion for new trial
Appellate jurisdiction and the issues presented on appeal

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Appellate Standards and the Structure of the Infringement Inquiry
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal framework the Federal Circuit used to evaluate the district court’s rulings. It clarifies the interaction between Federal Circuit patent law and Fifth Circuit procedural standards, and shows how claim construction, substantial-evidence review, and JMOL doctrine shape the court’s analysis of whether the jury’s infringement verdicts could stand.
subtopics: Why regional circuit law governs review of JMOL and new-trial rulings
Fifth Circuit standard for reviewing denial of JMOL de novo
Substantial evidence review of a jury’s infringement finding
Claim construction review: de novo with clear-error review for subsidiary factfinding
The plaintiff’s burden of proof on infringement at trial
How the court distinguishes between legal claim-scope questions and evidentiary sufficiency questions
The significance of expert testimony in proving infringement
Why self-contradictory expert testimony can fail as a matter of law

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: The ’134 Patent—Sampling Limitation, Expert Mapping, and Failure of Proof
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the Federal Circuit’s reversal as to the ’134 patent. It walks through the representative claim, focuses on limitation 1[a], and explains why Finesse’s infringement theory failed: its expert repeatedly mapped the claimed 'interference generating signals' to a modeled PIM path that was created only after sampling, making the required claim sequence impossible on the accused system as described at trial.
subtopics: The ’134 patent’s objective: reducing IMP interference by isolating and cancelling interference-generating signals
Representative claim 1 and the importance of limitation 1[a]
Claim requirement that the receiver over-sample a passband containing both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals'
Dr. Wells’s reliance on Nokia technical documents to identify claim elements in the accused radios
His express mapping of 'signals of interest' to the DL(TX) reference
His express mapping of 'interference generating signals' to the modeled PIM path
The critical temporal/architectural problem: the RF ADC cannot sample the modeled PIM path because that path is generated downstream after sampling
Cross-examination and the attempted pivot to x1 and x2
Why the court found the pivot unclear, incomplete, and never properly tied to the claim language
The district court’s effort to infer a workable theory from scattered testimony
The Federal Circuit’s rejection of inferential reconstruction of the expert’s testimony
Use of Johns Hopkins v. Datascope to explain why contradictory expert testimony cannot support literal infringement
Holding as to the ’134 patent: no substantial evidence, so denial of JMOL reversed

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: The ’775 Patent—Claim Scope, Prosecution History, and the Seven-Multiplication Requirement
outline.description: This chapter explains the separate path the court took for the ’775 patent. It first addresses claim construction and prosecution-history arguments about whether 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' must be unique. It then turns to the decisive issue: even under the district court’s construction, the trial evidence did not show that the accused radios performed the seven claimed multiplications.
subtopics: The ’775 patent’s objective: receiver-side cancellation of passive IMPs using transmitter-signal copies
Representative claim 1 and the detailed recitation of seven third-order multiplications
District court claim construction: 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' must be separately identifiable, not necessarily unique
Appellants’ argument that prosecution amendments surrendered systems using only two unique input signals
The examiner’s rejection over Filipovic and the amendment from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals'
Why the Federal Circuit found no clear and unambiguous disavowal of systems with two unique inputs
The court’s acceptance that the claim does not require three unique input signals
The decisive evidentiary issue: the claim still requires performance of seven listed multiplications
Dr. Wells’s infringement theory based on Nokia technical documents
The Nokia document’s actual operations: modulus and complex-conjugate expressions rather than the seven claimed products
The three distinct multiplications identified at trial
Why three distinct multiplications could not simply be treated as equivalent to the seven claimed multiplications without a trial-supported mapping
The absence of testimony explaining how the accused operations correspond to each of the seven recited claim terms
The court’s rejection of appellate-stage efforts to repair the mapping
The oral-argument reference to ten multiplications and why it did not cure the evidentiary deficiency
Holding as to the ’775 patent: no reasonable jury could find the seven-multiplication limitation satisfied

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: Disposition, Damages Consequences, and Lessons from the Opinion
outline.description: This chapter concludes with the court’s disposition and the practical significance of the ruling. It explains why the damages award could not survive once all infringement verdicts were undone, and highlights the opinion’s broader lessons about proof of infringement in technically complex patent cases.
subtopics: The relationship between liability findings and the damages award
Review of the district court’s denial of a new trial on damages under Fifth Circuit abuse-of-discretion standards
Why the Federal Circuit did not need to resolve the damages challenges independently after reversing infringement
Vacatur of the entire damages award as a consequence of noninfringement JMOL
Formal disposition: reversed and vacated, with costs to appellants
The opinion’s practical lesson on precision in expert claim mapping
The danger of relying on diagrams and labels without accounting for system timing and signal generation order
The difference between claim-construction success and evidentiary sufficiency at trial
How the case illustrates that appellate courts will not reconstruct an infringement theory the expert did not clearly present to the jury
